Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verses 7–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they said, "What is wrong with this Messenger? He eats food and walks in the markets."﴾ There are two interpretations:

The first: they said this as a belittling of him, that since he was in need of food like them and went about in the markets, it was not right that he should be distinguished over them by prophethood, and he must be like them in judgment.

The second: they said this seeking to increase him in status, as he had been given more distinction over them, so he should not need food like the angels, nor go about in the markets like kings.

Their intention in both interpretations is corrupt for two reasons:

The first: his being distinguished in rank does not require removing him from the original nature of creation, for two reasons:

The first: every kind may have members who excel in rank without this requiring their distinction in creation. Likewise is the case of one who is preferred in prophethood.

The second: if he were removed from the nature of his creation by being singled out with prophethood, he would become of a kind other than theirs, and would not be a messenger from among them, and this is something souls shun.

As for the second interpretation: prophethood does not require preventing him from walking in the markets, for two reasons:

The first: this is an act of tyrants, and Allah has preserved His Messenger from arrogance.

The second: he needs to call the people of the markets to his prophethood, and to observe what they are upon of wrongdoing which he prohibits and of good which he approves.

﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ meaning: why was an angel not sent down to him? In this there are two interpretations:

The first: that the angel would be a proof of his truthfulness.

The second: that it would be a minister for him, whose opinion he would consult.

﴿Or a treasure be thrown to him﴾, so that he would not be poor.

﴿Or he have a garden from which he eats﴾. A garden is an orchard. It is as if they considered him insignificant because of his poverty.

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, He only withheld it from His Prophet by choice, and He only spread it out for others as a deception. Were it not so, He would not have made him dependent."

(p-134) His saying: ﴿And the wrongdoers said﴾, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh. It was said that this was Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara.

﴿You only follow a man bewitched﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: he was bewitched, so his mind departed.

The second: meaning, he has bewitched you with what he says.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you﴾, meaning what has preceded of their statements.

﴿So they have gone astray﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: they went astray from the truth in coining them.

The second: they were inconsistent in mentioning them, for they said "he has fabricated it," then they said "it is dictated to him," and these two are contradictory.

﴿So they cannot find a way﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: a way out of the similitudes which they coined, as said by Mujahid.

The second: a way to obedience to Allah, as said by al-Suddi.

The third: a way to good, as said by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they are thrown into it, into a narrow place﴾. Abdullah ibn Amr said: "Indeed Hell will be so narrow upon the disbelievers like the narrowness of the spike upon the spear."

﴿Bound together﴾. In this there are two interpretations: the first: bound with their hands tied, as said by Abu Salih.

The second: each one of them is bound to his devil, as said by Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿There they will call out for destruction﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: woe, as said by Ibn Abbas.

(p-135) The second: ruin, as said by al-Dahhak.

The third: its meaning is "alas for us" and "turning away" from the obedience of Allah. This was related by Ibn Isa, and it was narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "The first to say it is Iblis."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?﴾ On this there are four opinions:

The first: it is the temptation of the poor by the rich, that he says, "If Allah had willed, He would have made me rich like him," and the blind man by the seeing, that he says, "If He had willed, He would have made me seeing like him," and the sick by the healthy, that he says, "If He had willed, He would have made me healthy like him." This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is a trial through transgression in the religion. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The third: that the trial is the patience of the prophets over the denial of their people. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The fourth: that it was revealed when Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Bilal, ʿAmir ibn Fuhayra, Salim the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, and others like them from among the poor freedmen embraced Islam. The mockers from Quraysh said: "Look at the followers of Muhammad from among our poor and our freedmen!" So this verse was revealed concerning them. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Regarding the word "trial" (fitnah) here, there are two meanings:

One: affliction (al-balaʾ).

The other: testing (al-ikhtibar).

﴿Will you be patient?﴾ meaning: regarding that with which you have been tested through this trial. In it there is an ellipsis, and its implied meaning is: "Or will you not be patient?"

الخامِسُ: أنَّهُ شِدَّةُ الكُفْرِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

قِيلَ أنَّ هَذِهِ الآيَةَ نَزَلَتْ في عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ أبِي أُمَيَّةَ بْنِ المُغِيرَةِ ومِكْرَزِ بْنِ حَفْصِ بْنِ الأخْنَفِ في جَماعَةٍ مِن قُرَيْشٍ قالُوا: لَوْلا أُنْزِلُ عَلَيْنا المَلائِكَةُ أوْ نَرى رَبَّنا.

فَنَزَلَ فِيهِمْ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يَوْمَ يَرَوْنَ المَلائِكَةَ﴾ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ:

أحَدُهُما: عِنْدَ المَوْتِ، قالَهُ يَحْيى بْنُ سَلّامٍ.

الثّانِي: يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

﴿لا بُشْرى يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ يَعْنِي بِالجَنَّةِ، قالَهُ عَطِيَّةُ العَوْفِيُّ: إذا كانَ يَوْمُ القِيامَةِ يُلْقى المُؤْمِنُ بِالبُشْرى فَإذا رَأى الكافِرُ ذَلِكَ تَمَنّاهُ فَلَمْ يَرَهُ مِنَ المَلائِكَةِ.

أحَدُها: مَعْناهُ مَعاذَ اللَّهِ أنْ تَكُونَ لَكُمُ البُشْرى يَوْمَئِذٍ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

الثّانِي: مَعْناهُ: مَنَعَنا أنْ نَصِلَ إلى شَيْءٍ مِنَ الخَيْرِ، قالَهُ عِكْرِمَةُ.

؎ حَنَّتْ إلى النَّخْلَةِ القُصْوى فَقُلْتُ لَها ∗∗∗ حَجْرٌ حَرامٌ إلّا تِلْكَ الدَّهارِيسَ.

(She yearned for the farthest palm tree, so I said to her: "Forbidden, prohibited, except for that bunch of dates.")

أحَدُهُما: أنَّهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ قالُوهُ لِلْكُفّارِ، قالَهُ الضَّحّاكُ.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُمُ الكُفّارُ قالُوهُ لِأنْفُسِهِمْ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

(The misguided Kharijites came upon the worshippers of their Lord and said: "Your blood is lawful to us.")

﴿إلى ما عَمِلُوا مِن عَمَلٍ﴾ فِيهِ قَوْلانِ:

أحَدُهُما: مِن عَمِلَ خَيْرًا لا يُتَقَبَّلُ مِنهم لِإحْباطِهِ بِالكُفْرِ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

الخامِسُ: أنَّهُ الرَّمادُ، قالَهُ عُبَيْدُ بْنُ يَعْلى.

أحَدُها: أنَّ المُسْتَقَرَّ في الجَنَّةِ والمَقِيلَ دُونَها، قالَهُ أبُو سِنانٍ.

الثّانِي: أنَّهُ عَنى مَوْضِعَ القائِلَةِ لِلدَّعَةِ وإنْ لَمْ يَقِيلُوا، ذَكَرَهُ ابْنُ عِيسى.

الثّالِثُ: أنَّهُ يَقِيلُ أوْلِياءَ اللَّهِ بَعْدَ الحِسابِ عَلى الأُسْرَةِ مَعَ الحُورِ العِينِ، ويَقِيلُ أعْداءَ اللَّهِ مَعَ الشَّياطِينِ المُقَرَّنِينَ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

(p-142) الرّابِعُ: لِأنَّهُ يَفْرَغُ مِن حِسابِهِمْ وقْتَ القائِلَةِ وهو نِصْفُ النَّهارِ، فَذَلِكَ أحْسَنُ مَقِيلًا، مِن مَقِيلِ الكُفّارِ، قالَهُ الفَرّاءُ.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verse 25–29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with the clouds﴾, concerning which there are two views:

The first: "with" means "upon" (ʿalā), as in "I shot with the bow" and "I shot from the bow." The intended meaning is the familiar cloud, the one below the sky, since it remains below it when the sky is split open.

The second view: it is a white cloud that is in the sky, which God sends down to His prophets, like the one that shaded the Children of Israel. He said, "in shadows of clouds," and the sky will split open and [the angels] will come out of it.

﴿And the angels will be sent down, a descending﴾, meaning that the angels will descend on that day, the Day of Assembly (yawm al-talāq), which is the day on which the people of the heavens and the people of the earth meet.

Concerning their descent there are two views:

The first: to give good news to the believer of Paradise and to the disbeliever of the Fire.

The second: so that with every soul there will be a driver and a witness.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾. It was said he is ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt.

﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger."﴾ Concerning this there are three aspects:

The first: "a way" means by obedience to God, as said by Qatada.

The second: a path to salvation, related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The third: a means of access to the Messenger, a connection to him, as said by al-Akhfash.

(p-143) ﴿"Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend."﴾ Concerning this there are three sayings:

The first: it means Satan, as said by Mujahid and Abu Raja.

The second: that it is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, as said by ʿAmr ibn Maymun.

The third: that it is Umayya ibn Khalaf, as said by al-Suddi. He mentioned that "the cause of this was that ʿUqba and Umayya were close friends, and ʿUqba used to frequent the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ). Umayya ibn Khalaf said to him: 'It has reached me that you have inclined towards the religion of Muhammad.' He said: 'I have not inclined.' He said: 'Then my face is forbidden to you until you go to him, spit in his face and disavow him.' So ʿUqba came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), spat on his face and disavowed him. This grieved the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so God revealed concerning him, informing of what he would come to: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer [will bite his hands]﴾ and the verse that follows it."

"So-and-so" is not made dual or plural.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the Messenger says: "My Lord, my people have certainly taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾ In it there are three interpretations:

The second: they spoke about it with hajr, meaning foul speech. This was said by Mujahid.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verses 32–34:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ Concerning the speakers of this among the disbelievers, there are two opinions:

(p-١٤٤) The first: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are the Jews, when they saw the Qur'an being sent down in parts. They said: "Why was it not sent down to him all at once, as the Torah was sent down to Musa (Moses)?"

﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

The first: so that We may encourage your heart through it, because it is a miracle that indicates your truthfulness. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Suddi.

The second: its meaning is: thus We sent it down in parts so that We might make it firm in your heart.

And there are two interpretations of this:

The first: because he was unlettered, and the Qur'an was not sent down to him in writing. Therefore its being sent down in parts was more firmly fixed in his heart and clung more closely to his heart.

The second: so that We may make your heart firm through the continuity of revelation and the constant descent of the Qur'an, so that you do not become lonely through the cessation of revelation.

﴿And We recited it with measured recitation (tartilan)﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations:

The first: "We sent it in order, one thing after another." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: "We divided it into parts, dividing it." This was said by Ibrahim.

The third: "We explained it in detail." This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: "We interpreted it with interpretation." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: "We made it clear with clarification." This was said by Qatada.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Ibn ʿAbbas, when you recite the Qur'an, recite it with tartil." I said: "And what is tartil?" He said: "Make it clear with clarification, do not cut it off abruptly like the cutting of a dry date-stalk (dagal), do not rush through it like the rushing of poetry, and let not the concern of any one of you be the end of the surah." Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verses 35–40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾ — concerning it there are four opinions:

First: that the Rass is the mine (ma'dan). This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

Second: that it is a village of the villages of al-Yamama called al-Fajj, belonging to Thamud. This was said by Qatada.

Third: that it is the area between Najran and Yemen up to Hadramawt. This was said by some of the exegetes (mufassirun).

Fourth: that it is the well.

And concerning the well there are three opinions:

First: that it is a well in Adharbayjan. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: that it is the well in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed at Antioch of Syria. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Third: that every well that is dug and not lined with stone is a rass. Zuhayr said:

They came early in the morning and entered in the heat of the day, so they and the Wadi al-Rass are like a hand in the mouth.

Concerning the companions of the Rass there are four opinions:

First: that they are the people of Shu'ayb. This was related by some of the exegetes.

Second: that they are a people who buried (rassa) their prophet in a well. This was said by Ikrima.

Third: that they are a people who were camping beside a well, worshipping idols, and whenever they did not overpower anyone who opposed their religion, they would kill him and throw him into it; and the Rass was in Syria. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: that they are a people to whom God sent a prophet, and they ate him, and they were the first people whose women practiced sorcery. This was said by al-Kalbi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they had certainly passed by the town﴾ — which is Sodom, the town of Lot.

﴿Which was rained upon with a rain of evil﴾ — the stones with which they were rained upon. And those who passed by it were the Quraysh.

﴿Had they not been seeing it?﴾ — that is, taking heed from it.

﴿Rather, they were not expecting resurrection﴾ — that is, they did not fear being raised up.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verses 41–44:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen one who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ On this there are three opinions:

The first: They are a people among whom a man would worship a stone that he found pleasing, and when he saw something better than it, he would worship that and abandon the first. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: It refers to al-Harith ibn Qays, who, whenever he desired something, would worship it. This is related by al-Naqqash.

The third: It refers to the one who follows his desire in everything it calls him to. This is said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿Would you then be a guardian over him?﴾ On this there are four interpretations:

The first: It means a protector (nasir). This is said by Qatadah.

The second: A preserver (hafiz). This is said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: A guarantor (kafil). This is said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: A controller (musaytir). This is said by al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verses 45–47:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord, how He extends the shadow?﴾ That is, spreads it over the earth. In this there are two views:

The first: the shadow is the night, because it is the shadow of the earth; it approaches with the sunset and recedes with the sunrise.

The second: it is the shadow of the day, by what is screened off from the rays of the sun.

Regarding the difference between al-Zill (shadow) and al-Fay' (the shade that returns after noon), there are two views:

The first: al-Zill is what is before the sunrise, and al-Fay' is what is after its rising.

The second: al-Zill is what is before the zawal (the sun's decline after its zenith), and al-Fay' is what is after it.

﴿Then We withdraw it to Us﴾, meaning the shadow. In this there are two views:

The first: He withdrew the shadow with the rising of the sun.

The second: with its setting.

﴿A gradual withdrawal﴾. In this there are three views:

The first: swift, related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: easy, related from Abu Malik.

The third: imperceptible, related from Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He made the night for you as a garment﴾, meaning a covering, because it conceals as clothing conceals.

﴿And sleep as rest (subat)﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: because one is cut off in it (masbut fihi), and the sleeper does not perceive like the dead; related by al-Naqqash.

The second: meaning rest from work, and from it the day of Saturday (al-Sabt) is named, because it is a day of rest from work; related by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿And He made the day a resurrection (nushur)﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: because the spirit disperses (intishar) in it through wakefulness; it is derived from nashr (spreading out) and ba'th (raising).

The second: because people disperse (intishar) in their livelihoods; related by Mujahid and Qatadah.

God's words: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾, meaning in what they invite you to: either in venerating their gods, or in making a truce with them.

The second: the sea of Persia and the sea of the Romans. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: that the barzakh is the boundaries; this is the saying of Qatadah.

"Mahjur" means "prevented" (mamnu').

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verse 61–62:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky great constellations (burujan)﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations:

The first: they are the great stars. This is the saying of Abu Salih.

The second: they are palaces in the sky in which there are guards. This is the saying of Atiyyah al-Awfi.

The third: they are the positions of the planets.

The fourth: they are the mansions of the sun. It is also read as burjan (with the vowel on the ba' and the jim as a singular form), which Qatadah recited, and he interpreted it as "the star."

﴿And a luminous moon (qamaran muniran)﴾: meaning, shining. For this reason He made the sun a lamp (siraj) and the moon a light (nur). Because the moon, when it is joined to the light of the sun and the blaze of its heat, is described as a lamp for the sake of heat, but when that quality is absent from the moon, He made it a light (nur).

﴿And He it is who made the night and the day alternating (khilfah)﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations:

The first: He made whatever of one of them's work was missed to be made up in the other. This was said by Umar ibn al-Khattab and al-Hasan.

The second: He made each of them different from its companion, so He made one white and the other black. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: each of them succeeds its companion; when this one passes, that one comes. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr:

*In it are the gazelles and the wild cattle walking in succession, and their young ones rising up from every resting place.*

﴿For whoever desires to be mindful﴾: that is, he prays by day the prayer of the night and prays by night the prayer of the day.

﴿Or desires gratitude (shukuran)﴾: this is the supererogatory prayer after the obligatory one. It was also said that this verse was revealed concerning Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

(p-155) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

First: they are scholars and [knowledgeable] people, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: they are chaste and God-fearing, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Third: they are [characterized] by tranquillity (al-sakīna) and dignity (al-waqār), said by Mujahid.

Fourth: they are humble and do not act arrogantly, said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. Concerning "the ignorant" (al-jāhilūn) there are two opinions:

One: they are the disbelievers.

The second: they are the foolish.

﴿They say, "Peace"﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects:

One: they say "sound words" (sadādan), said by Mujahid, because it is a sound (salīm) speech.

The second: they say, "And upon you be peace," said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The third: it is a request for peaceful dealing (al-musālama), said by Ibn Baḥr.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, its punishment is ever a relentless torment (gharāman)﴾. Concerning this there are four aspects:

One: "constant" (lāziman), said by Ibn ʿĪsā, and from this comes the word al-gharīm (creditor/debtor), because of its persistence (mulāzama). He recited al-Aʿshā:

"If it punishes, it will be relentless (gharāman), and if it gives abundantly, it does not care."

The second: "severe" (shadīdan), said by Ibn Shajara, and from this the severity of a trial is called gharām. Bishr ibn Abī Khāzim said:

"The Day of al-Jifār and the Day of al-Nisār, they were a punishment and were gharām."

The third: "heavy" (thaqīlan), said by Qutrub, and from this the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then they will be burdened with a heavy debt (maghram)﴾ [al-Qalam: 46].

The fourth: they were made to pay for their pleasures in the world with the punishment of the Fire. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: God asked the disbelievers about [their wealth] and then made them pay for it, so He admitted them into Hell.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who, when they spend, neither are extravagant﴾. Concerning this there are four aspects:

One: they do not spend in disobedience to God, and extravagance (al-isrāf) is spending on sins, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they do not spend much so that people would say they have been extravagant, said by Ibrahim.

The third: they do not eat food seeking luxury, nor wear clothing seeking adornment, said by Yazid ibn Abī Ḥabīb, who said: "These were the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, whose hearts were upon the heart of one man."

The fourth: they do not spend money in other than its right place, for spending in other than its right place is extravagance, said by Ibn Sīrīn.

﴿Nor are they niggardly﴾. Concerning this there are four aspects:

One: they do not withhold God's rights, for withholding God's rights is niggardliness (iqtār), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they do not leave them naked or hungry, said by Ibrahim.

The third: they do not withhold themselves from obedience to God, said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: they do not fall short in what is right, said by al-Aʿmash.

Muʿadh ibn Jabal narrated: "When this verse was revealed, I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about what constitutes extravagance and niggardliness in spending. He said: 'Whoever withholds from what is right has been niggardly, and whoever gives in what is not right has been extravagant.'"

﴿And between that is a balance (qawāman)﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects:

One: it means justice (ʿadlan), said by al-Aʿmash.

The second: qawām means that they give up half of their wealth for God, said by Wahb.

The third: qawām means that they spend in the obedience of God and refrain from the prohibitions of God.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: qawām is that in which nothing precious is withheld and one does not venture into danger. The difference between qawām with a fatḥa (qawām) and qawām with a kasra (qiwām), according to what Thaʿlab said, is that with the fatḥa it means uprightness and justice, while with the kasra it means that which the matter endures and becomes settled upon.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent these to Wahshi, and [Wahshi] came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, meaning they do not make a partner (shari'k) for Allah, may He be exalted, nor do they set up any intermediary between themselves and Him in worship (wasit).

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾, meaning He has forbidden its killing, and it is the soul of a believer and of a mu'ahad (a non-Muslim under a covenant of protection).

﴿Except by right﴾. The right by which its killing is made permissible is what has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The blood of a Muslim man is not lawful except in one of three cases: apostasy after faith, adultery after being muhsan (married), or killing a soul without a soul [in retaliation]."

﴿And do not commit adultery﴾. Zina (adultery, fornication) is having intercourse with forbidden women, whether in the front or the back passage. Sodomy (liwat) is zina according to one of the two opinions, and according to the second opinion it necessitates the death penalty for both the one who does it and the one to whom it is done. Regarding intercourse with animals there are three opinions:

First: it is like zina in distinguishing between a virgin (bikr) and a previously married person (thayyib).

Second: it necessitates the killing of the animal and of the one who had intercourse with it, on account of the transmitted report concerning it.

Third: it necessitates ta'zir (discretionary punishment).

Thus in this verse He combined three of the grave sins: shirk, killing a soul, and zina. 'Amr ibn Shurahbil related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah' (or he said, 'Someone other than me said'): 'Which sin is greatest in the sight of Allah?' He said: '(That you set up a rival (nidd) to Allah while He created you).' He said: 'Then which?' He said: '(That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you).' He said: 'Then which?' He said: '(That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife).'" He said: "Then Allah revealed that."

﴿And whoever does that﴾, meaning these three or some of them, ﴿will meet a penalty (athama)﴾. Concerning athama there are three views:

First: that athama means punishment. This was said by Bal'am ibn Qays:

"May Allah recompense Ibn 'Urwa, since he has become one who disobeys his parents by evening, and disobedience to parents brings a penalty (athama) upon him."

Second: that athama is the name of a valley in Hell. This was said by Ibn 'Umar and Qatada, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I met destruction in our war, and after destruction you will meet athama."

Third: that it is recompense. This was said by al-Suddi, and the poet said:

"Indeed our station is that we call down curses upon you at Abtah, at Dhu al-Majaz, where there is an athama for you."

﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Concerning this there are three views:

First: that the doubling is the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. This was said by Qatada.

Second: that it is the combining of the punishments for the grave sins which have gathered together.

Third: that it is the continuation of punishment through remaining in it forever.

﴿And he will abide therein﴾, meaning he will abide forever in the punishment for shirk.

﴿Humiliated (muhanan)﴾ by the punishment.

﴿Except one who repents﴾, meaning from zina.

﴿And believes﴾, meaning from shirk.

﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, meaning after the evil deeds.

﴿Then those—Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: in this world, He replaces for them shirk with faith, zina with chastity (ihsan), remembrance of Allah after forgetfulness, and obedience to Him after disobedience. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Hasan and Qatada.

Second: that it refers to the Hereafter, concerning one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds, so Allah replaces the evil deeds with good deeds. This was said by Abu Hurayra.

Third: that Allah replaces the punishment for his evil deeds, when he repents from them, with the reward for his good deeds when he turns to them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what preceded before repentance.

﴿Merciful﴾ toward what follows it.

Al-Kalbi related that Wahshi, who was a slave of 'Utba ibn Ghazwan, wrote after the Battle of Uhud and the killing of Hamza, to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is there any repentance? For Allah has sent down in Mecca that I have despaired of every good: ﴿And those who do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾, the verse." And indeed Wahshi did all of this: he committed zina, associated partners with Allah, and killed a soul which Allah had forbidden. So Allah revealed: ﴿Except one who repents﴾, meaning from zina, and believes after shirk, and does righteous deeds after the evil deeds. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote these to him. Wahshi said: "This is a severe condition, and perhaps I will not live after repentance long enough to do righteous deeds." So he wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is there anything more comprehensive than this?" Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:48, 116]. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote these to Wahshi.

Then Wahshi sent to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed I fear that I may not be within the will of Allah." Then Allah revealed concerning Wahshi and his companions: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾ [az-Zumar 39:53], the verse.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent these to Wahshi, and [Wahshi] came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 25, verse 72–74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not witness falsehood﴾. Concerning it there are seven interpretations:

First: It is shirk (associating partners with God). This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

Second: It is the festivals of the People of the Dhimma (non-Muslim protected subjects) and the like. Ibn Sirin said: it is al-Sha'anin (a Christian festival of palm/Palm Sunday).

Third: It is singing (al-ghina'). This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: It is gatherings of obscenity (al-khana). This was said by Amr ibn Qays.

Fifth: It is play (la'ib) that was practiced in the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic period). This was said by Ikrima.

Sixth: It is lying (al-kadhib). This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Qatada.

Seventh: It is a gathering in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was reviled. This was said by Khalid ibn Kathir.

It may also be taken as an eighth: it is covenants upon acts of disobedience.

﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾. Concerning it there are five interpretations:

First: It is what the polytheists would do of harming the Muslims in their persons and honour, so they turn away from them and from their harm. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: When they mention marriage (al-nikah), they speak of it by allusion. This was related by al-Awwam.

Third: When they mention the private parts (al-furuj), they speak of them by allusion. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ali al-Baqir, may God have mercy on him.

Fourth: When they pass by the falsehood of the polytheists, they deny it. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: That idle talk here refers to all acts of disobedience, and their passing by them with dignity is their turning away from them. This was said by al-Hasan.

It may also be taken as a sixth: when they pass by jesting, they turn from it to seriousness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord﴾. It may have two meanings:

One: by His promise and His threat.

The second: by His command and His prohibition.

﴿they do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾. That is: they hear the admonition and do not turn deaf to it, and they see the right guidance and do not become blind to it, unlike one whom shirk has made deaf to admonition and error has made blind to right guidance.

Concerning His saying, ﴿they do not fall upon them﴾, there are two meanings:

One: they do not establish them (i.e., do not stand firm in them). This was said by al-Akhfash.

The second: they do not feign heedlessness. This was said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and our offspring comfort of the eyes﴾. Concerning it there are two meanings:

One: make our spouses and our offspring a comfort of the eyes. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: grant us from our spouses and from our offspring helpers ﴿comfort of the eyes﴾, that is, people of obedience, by whom our eyes are cooled in this world through righteousness, and in the Hereafter through Paradise.

Concerning qurrat al-'ayn (comfort of the eyes) there are two meanings:

(p-161) One: that one meets what pleases them, so the eye rests on looking at it and nothing else.

The second: that al-qarr is coldness, so its meaning is that God cools their tears, for the tear of joy is cold, while the tear of [sorrow] is hot. The opposite of qurrat al-'ayn is suhnat al-'ayn (heat of the eye). This was said by al-Asma'i.

﴿And make us a model for the God-fearing﴾. Concerning it there are five aspects:

First: examples (amthal). This was said by Ikrima.

Second: contentment (ridan). This was said by Ja'far al-Sadiq.

Third: leaders to good (qadah ila al-khayr). This was said by Qatada.

Fourth: leaders of guidance by whom people are guided. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Fifth: that we follow those before us so that those after us may follow us. This was said by Mujahid.

In the verse there is evidence that seeking leadership in religion is recommended (nadb).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on surah 25, verses 75–77:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber﴾ have two interpretations:

The first: the lofty chamber is Paradise. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The second: it is the highest and most excellent of the dwellings of Paradise, just as the lofty chamber is the highest of the dwellings of this world. This is related by Ibn Shajara.

﴿for what they endured with patience﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: for what they endured with patience against the desires. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The second: for what they endured with patience in obeying Allah.

﴿and they will be met therein with greeting﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: it means lasting eternity.

The second: it means a great dominion.

﴿and peace﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: it comprises all security and goodness.

(p-162) The second: it is that some of them greet others with peace. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

For the people of the *khawatir* (inner reflections and insights) regarding the greeting and the peace, there are two interpretations:

The first: the greeting is for the spirit and the peace is for the body.

The second: the greeting is for the intellect and the peace is for the soul.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you﴾ have two interpretations:

The first: what He would do with you. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: what He would heed. This is the view of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

﴿were it not for your calling (upon Him)﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: were it not for your worship and your faith in Him, for *du'a'* (calling) here means worship.

The second: were it not for His calling you to obedience. This is the view of Mujahid.

It may also admit a third meaning: were it not for your calling upon Him when harm touches you and misfortune befalls you, out of desire for Him and humility before Him.

﴿For you have denied﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: you denied My messengers.

The second: you fell short in obeying Me, taken from their saying "he denied in the battle" when he fell short.

﴿inevitable punishment﴾ has four interpretations:

The first: it is the punishment of this world, namely the killing on the day of Badr. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy.

The second: it is the punishment of the Hereafter on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of Qatada.

The third: it is death. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"He turns away at the time of her need, the bearer of glad tidings,
and I did not flinch from the inescapable death."

The fourth: it is the binding of the proof in the Hereafter upon their denial in this world. This is the view of al-Dahhak. The most apparent of these interpretations is that *lizam* (inevitable) means the requital, because it is necessarily bound to them. And Allah knows best.
